claims.claim: Hong Kong should not impose a hard cap on initial rents for subdivided units.
A hard cap targets the price of a symptom while leaving the public-housing queue untouched.
The households most in need would bear the cost of rental-market contraction.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped increases within tenancies but left initial rents untouched.
The stock index grew from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025.
First-generation rent controls show consistent contraction effects while second-generation controls show small or null effects.
The Hong Kong ordinance is second-generation, so its visible stability is an artifact of a non-binding instrument.
A 10 percent cap-induced reduction in initial rents would remove roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years.
A 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about 900 dollars per month to incumbents.
Such a cut would leave 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households.
A policy helping incumbents while shutting out new entrants is regressive.
Berlin illustrates that caps bind differently on new entrants than incumbents, with the bill handed to those outside.
Current inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year.
A band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years.
Enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tenants, such as those with no written agreement or newest arrivals.
No design was identified under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last.
Mr Chan names the waiting list, not rent, as what would help most.
In an NGO survey of 440 households, 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year tenure security and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer.
The binding constraint is queue length and insecurity, not price level.
The Landlords Association's exit threat is self-interested and its data thin, but academic elasticity estimates do not depend on it.
A published, indexed, reviewable per-square-foot band framed as rate-capping is a defensible middle instrument.
The NGO report supports tenure security plus a light band on initial rents and opposes a hard cap.
The consultation document appears to float a floor-standard plus rent band package rather than a hard cap.
The counterargument that 2021 stability shows capacity for more control misreads the evidence because the instrument was non-binding at first rent.
Hong Kong should secure tenure, publish bands, and above all shorten the public-housing queue.

cites.sentence: The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped increases within tenancies but left initial rents untouched [D1p3].
The stock index shows continued growth through that period, from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025 [D2p1].

The working paper explains that first-generation controls show consistent contraction effects, while second-generation controls show small or null effects—and the Hong Kong ordinance is second-generation [D6p2].
A binding cap on initial rents would behave differently: the reviewed elasticity band suggests a 10 percent cap-induced reduction removes roughly 3 to 5 percent of stock over five years [D6p1].

The working paper's model of a 15 percent cut in initial rents yields a net transfer of about 900 dollars per month to incumbents, against 3,000 to 4,000 households per year unable to enter the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households [D6p4].
These are precisely the populations named in the primer as the segment's core tenants [D1p2].
Berlin illustrates the mechanism: caps bind differently on new entrants than incumbents, and the bill is handed to those still outside [D7p3].

Current inspection capacity covers under 6 percent of stock per year, and a band-based initial-rent cap would require a certifiable tenancy register estimated at 40 to 60 staff-years to stand up [D10p1].

More damning, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], or the newest arrivals—so enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].

More damning, the tenants least able to complain are those with no written agreement, like Mrs Wong [D4p1], or the newest arrivals—so enforcement would systematically miss the most exploited tail [D10p2].
The subcommittee could not identify any design under which the newest-arrival tail is protected first rather than last [D10p3].
Mr Chan, asked what would help most, does not name rent—he names the waiting list, saying he would accept any rent to leave if the queue were three years instead of five and a half [D3p3].
The NGO survey of 440 households finds 61 percent would trade a nominal rent increase for three-year security of tenure, and 74 percent for a faster public-housing offer [D11p1].

Mrs Wong supports a hard cap, but her own account contains the contradiction the archive flags: she reports two flats converted to non-residential storage after the ordinance while still believing landlords cannot exit [D4p3].
The Landlords Association's threat to exit [D5p2]

is self-interested and its data thin—no margin data, a 34 percent response rate on self-reported costs [D5p3]—but the academic elasticity estimates do not depend on taking the Association at its word.
The legal opinion points to a defensible middle instrument: a published per-square-foot band, indexed and reviewable, framed as rate-capping rather than confiscation [D9p2].
The NGO report supports exactly this—tenure security plus a light band on initial rents, opposing a hard cap [D11p3].
The consultation document already appears to be floating a "floor-standard + rent band" package rather than a hard cap [D12p1].
This is the right direction: it addresses insecurity, which tenants name as the real harm [D3p1][D11p1], without triggering the contraction arithmetic that would fall on new arrivals.
This is the right direction: it addresses insecurity, which tenants name as the real harm [D3p1][D11p1], without triggering the contraction arithmetic that would fall on new arrivals.
The strongest counterargument is that the 2021 ordinance's stability shows capacity for more control [D12p2].
But that argument misreads the evidence: the instrument was non-binding at first-rent, which is exactly why stock stayed stable [D6p2].
The uncomfortable welfare arithmetic of contraction [D6p3]
